power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed cancer treatment, yet evidence on their utilization, treatment trajectories, and effectiveness in routine clinical practice remains limited.
We characterized real-world ICI use and outcomes across cancer types using the multicenter FAIR-ICI cohort and explored differences between real-world and pivotal trial outcomes.
We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults receiving ICIs across four Belgian hospitals.
Structured and unstructured electronic health record data were harmonized using the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model (OMOP-CDM) and natural language processing.
We evaluated overall survival (OS), time on treatment (ToT), time to next treatment (TTNT), ICI discontinuation (>12-week treatment gap without re-initiation), and post-discontinuation survival.
text.formatted: We evaluated overall survival (OS), time on treatment (ToT), time to next treatment (TTNT), ICI discontinuation (>12-week treatment gap without re-initiation), and post-discontinuation survival.

text.text: OS was descriptively compared with pivotal trials, and prognostic factors were assessed using multivariable Cox regression.
An interactive public dashboard was developed to enable exploration of cohort characteristics, treatment patterns, and outcomes.
Results: Among 3,231 ICI-treated patients, 2,514 (77.8%) had metastatic disease.
Among metastatic patients, 568 (22.6%) discontinued ICI without subsequent systemic therapy.
Median post-discontinuation OS was 21.4 months (95% CI 16.5-37.2), with 49.1% alive at 24 months.
ToT and TTNT were generally shorter than OS, particularly in melanoma (median OS 78 months; ToT 7 months; TTNT 26 months).
Real-world survival was frequently less favorable than in pivotal trials.
ECOG ≥2 was associated with poorer OS than ECOG 0-1 (adjusted HR 2.18, 95% CI 1.82-2.60).
In NSCLC patients receiving pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy, survival with ECOG 0-1 more closely approximated trial outcomes, whereas survival with ECOG ≥2 was substantially poorer.
Conclusions: Real-world ICI treatment trajectories extend beyond active treatment, with some patients experiencing prolonged survival after discontinuation.
Differences between real-world and trial outcomes highlight the importance of patient characteristics, particularly performance status, when interpreting trial evidence in routine care.
FAIR-ICI provides a scalable framework for evaluating real-world immunotherapy effectiveness, treatment trajectories, and future investigations of treatment-related toxicity.
Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed cancer treatment, improving survival and becoming standard-of-care across multiple malignancies.

Since the European Medicines Agency (EMA) approved ipilimumab for metastatic melanoma in 2011 1 , ICI indications have expanded rapidly across tumor types, disease stages, and treatment combinations 2, 3 .
text.formatted: Since the European Medicines Agency (EMA) approved ipilimumab for metastatic melanoma in 2011 <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> , ICI indications have expanded rapidly across tumor types, disease stages, and treatment combinations <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: Recent estimates indicate that approximately 57% of patients with advanced or metastatic cancer may be eligible for ICI treatment 4 , highlighting the growing role of ICIs in contemporary oncology care.
text.formatted: Recent estimates indicate that approximately 57% of patients with advanced or metastatic cancer may be eligible for ICI treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> , highlighting the growing role of ICIs in contemporary oncology care.

text.text: Belgium, with around 77,000 new cancer diagnoses annually 5 , provides an informative setting for evaluating real-world ICI use.
text.formatted: Belgium, with around 77,000 new cancer diagnoses annually <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> , provides an informative setting for evaluating real-world ICI use.

text.text: Since 2017, an accelerated reimbursement pathway has enabled access to ICIs immediately following EMA approval, rather than through the conventional Belgian reimbursement procedure 6 , with ICIs currently reimbursed across 23 cancer types 7 .
text.formatted: Since 2017, an accelerated reimbursement pathway has enabled access to ICIs immediately following EMA approval, rather than through the conventional Belgian reimbursement procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> , with ICIs currently reimbursed across 23 cancer types <ref type="bibr">7</ref> .

text.text: A recent European Comparator Report ranked Belgium among countries with the highest ICI uptake (roughly six standard weekly doses per incident cancer case) 8 .
text.formatted: A recent European Comparator Report ranked Belgium among countries with the highest ICI uptake (roughly six standard weekly doses per incident cancer case) <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">8</ref> .

text.text: At current Belgian list prices, this corresponds to an estimated drug cost of approximately €10,800 per incident cancer case.
As ICI use continues to expand globally, evidence from this setting can inform understanding of real-world treatment patterns, effectiveness, and resource implications across healthcare systems.

Despite widespread use, evidence supporting ICIs remains largely derived from randomized controlled trials (RCTs), whose populations and treatment pathways may not reflect routine clinical practice 9 .
text.formatted: Despite widespread use, evidence supporting ICIs remains largely derived from randomized controlled trials (RCTs), whose populations and treatment pathways may not reflect routine clinical practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">9</ref> .

text.text: Previous studies have estimated that approximately 70% of NSCLC patients were not eligible for pivotal phase III ICI trials 10 .
text.formatted: Previous studies have estimated that approximately 70% of NSCLC patients were not eligible for pivotal phase III ICI trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">10</ref> .

text.text: Such differences may contribute to the efficacy-effectiveness gap between clinical trials and real-world populations.

Furthermore, RCTs provide limited insight into treatment trajectories, including treatment duration, discontinuation, and transitions to subsequent therapy 11, 12 , which are important for understanding clinical decision-making, patient outcomes, and healthcare resource use.
text.formatted: Furthermore, RCTs provide limited insight into treatment trajectories, including treatment duration, discontinuation, and transitions to subsequent therapy <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">12</ref> , which are important for understanding clinical decision-making, patient outcomes, and healthcare resource use.

text.text: Real-world evidence (RWE) complements clinical trials by evaluating treatment use and outcomes in routine practice 13 .
text.formatted: Real-world evidence (RWE) complements clinical trials by evaluating treatment use and outcomes in routine practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">13</ref> .

text.text: However, comprehensive multicenter studies spanning multiple tumor types remain limited, often constrained by fragmented data sources and insufficient clinical detail 14 .
text.formatted: However, comprehensive multicenter studies spanning multiple tumor types remain limited, often constrained by fragmented data sources and insufficient clinical detail <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">14</ref> .

text.text: Most studies focus primarily on overall survival (OS), whereas treatment-trajectory endpoints such as time on treatment (ToT) and time to next treatment (TTNT) are less frequently reported.
Similarly, little is known about treatment discontinuation patterns, including the proportion of patients discontinuing ICIs without subsequent systemic treatment and their survival.

To address these challenges, the FAIR-ICI cohort was established as a multicenter Belgian real-world dataset integrating structured and unstructured electronic health record (EHR) data within a standardized Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model (OMOP-CDM) framework 15, 16 .
text.formatted: To address these challenges, the FAIR-ICI cohort was established as a multicenter Belgian real-world dataset integrating structured and unstructured electronic health record (EHR) data within a standardized Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model (OMOP-CDM) framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">16</ref> .

text.text: Natural language processing (NLP) enriches structured data with clinically relevant information extracted from routine records.

By combining multicenter patient-level data, standardized data harmonization, and NLP-enriched clinical information, FAIR-ICI enables high-resolution evaluation of ICI utilization, treatment trajectories, and outcomes across routine oncology practice.

In this study, we aimed to (1) assess patient demographics, disease characteristics, and treatment patterns among patients receiving ICIs; (2) estimate real-world outcomes, including OS, TTNT, and ToT; (3) characterize treatment discontinuation patterns and survival following discontinuation; and (4) compare real-world survival with pivotal clinical trials.
To facilitate transparent exploration, we additionally developed an interactive dashboard that enables dynamic subgroup analyses and visualization of outcomes.

Together, these analyses provide a comprehensive overview of ICI use and effectiveness in routine oncology care and establish FAIR-ICI as a platform for future research on immunotherapy-related toxicity.

This multicenter, retrospective observational cohort study used routinely collected EHR data from four Belgian hospitals: two academic centers (University Hospital Antwerp and University Hospital Brussels) and two regional hospitals (Maria Middelares Hospital Ghent and AZ Groeninge Hospital Kortrijk).
All institutions maintain OMOP-CDM version 5 databases generated through standardized extract-transform-load (ETL) procedures.

The study period extended from September 2015 to November 2024 and covered all available data, with start and end dates varying across data partners and data sources (start date ranging from September 2015 to January 2018, and end date from November 2023 to November 2024).

The FAIR-ICI database integrates structured data (hospital cancer registries, medication administration records, laboratory measurements, administrative datasets, and minimal hospital data-mandatory Belgian reporting datasets containing harmonized administrative and diagnostic information) and unstructured clinical text (tumor board reports, consultation notes, pathology reports, radiology reports, and discharge summaries).
Unstructured clinical text was processed using a previously developed NLP pipeline 17 .
text.formatted: Unstructured clinical text was processed using a previously developed NLP pipeline <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">17</ref> .

text.text: NLP-derived clinical concepts were mapped to Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) Concept Unique Identifiers (CUIs) and subsequently converted to standardized OMOP concept identifiers using OMOP Athena vocabularies.
Structured and NLP-derived variables were transformed into the OMOP-CDM.
The data extraction and processing workflow is illustrated in Supplementary-Figure S1.
text.formatted: The data extraction and processing workflow is illustrated in Supplementary-Figure <ref type="figure">S1</ref>.

text.text: Supplementary-Tables S1-S3 provide the datapoint list (including source systems, OMOP tables, and UMLS CUIs), data dictionary (variable definitions, derivation logic, timing, and data sources), and NLP performance metrics, respectively.
text.formatted: Supplementary-Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S1-S3</ref> provide the datapoint list (including source systems, OMOP tables, and UMLS CUIs), data dictionary (variable definitions, derivation logic, timing, and data sources), and NLP performance metrics, respectively.

text.text: Data were pseudonymized before ETL processing.
The study population included adult patients who initiated ICI treatment during the study period.
The index event was defined as the first ICI administration.

Eligible ICIs, available in Belgium during the study period, included PD-1 inhibitors (nivolumab, pembrolizumab, cemiplimab, and dostarlimab), PD-L1 inhibitors (atezolizumab, durvalumab, and avelumab), and CTLA-4 inhibitors (ipilimumab and tremelimumab), either as monotherapy or in approved combination regimens.
To make sure we only included new ICI users, patients were required to have at least 183 days of prior observation, except when cancer diagnosis occurred within 21 days before the index.

Patients were followed from the index date until cohort exit, which happened at death, diagnosis of a second primary malignancy, initiation of a new ICI regimen, ICI re-initiation after a gap exceeding 12 weeks, or end of available data.
Cancer type was assigned using structured cancer records and NLP-derived diagnoses, considering reimbursed ICI indications (Supplementary-Methods S1; Figure S2).
text.formatted: Cancer type was assigned using structured cancer records and NLP-derived diagnoses, considering reimbursed ICI indications (Supplementary-Methods S1; Figure <ref type="figure">S2</ref>).

text.text: Tumor stage at diagnosis and ICI initiation was determined using TNM staging and metastasis-related information (Supplementary-Methods S2).

Baseline variables included demographic characteristics (age, sex, body mass index [BMI]), lifestyle factors (smoking status and alcohol abuse), Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status, tumor type, and stage at ICI initiation.
Treatment characteristics included ICI initiation year, ICI agent, mechanism of action, and regimen classification.

Regimen type was determined according to all systemic anticancer therapies administered on the index date and categorized as ICI monotherapy, dual ICI therapy, ICI plus chemotherapy, ICI plus tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), or other ICI-containing combinations.
Patients were considered to be on treatment until 12 weeks after last ICI administration or initiation of a new systemic antineoplastic regimen, whichever occurred first.
A gap exceeding 12 weeks was considered permanent discontinuation of the index treatment episode.
Treatment status at data cut off was classified as ongoing treatment, death during treatment, switch to a new systemic anticancer regimen, or permanent discontinuation.
The primary time-to-event outcomes were OS, ToT, and TTNT.
OS was defined as the time from the index date to death from any cause, based on linkage to hospital and governmental death records.
Patients without a registered death date were censored at the last recorded observation.
ToT was defined as the time from the index date to treatment-ending events, including death, initiation of a new systemic anticancer regimen, or permanent discontinuation of the index ICI regimen.
TTNT was defined as the time from the index date to initiation of a new systemic treatment regimen not part of the initial combination regimen.
The event date was defined as the first administration of the new regimen.
Switching to another ICI or addition of chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or hormonal therapy was considered a next treatment.
Death was treated as a censoring event.

Data quality was assessed through a multilayered validation framework: data intake validation, NLP validation, clinical validation of individual datapoints, and clinical validation of aggregated outputs.

During data intake validation, participating hospitals verified completeness and coverage of source datasets through checks for missing values, date inconsistencies, duplicate records, and compliance with inclusion criteria.
LynxCare Clinical Informatics evaluated NLP-derived variables against human-annotated reference datasets, calculating precision, recall, and F1 scores for each datapoint.
Models were iteratively refined until predefined performance targets were achieved (Supplementary-Table S3).
text.formatted: Models were iteratively refined until predefined performance targets were achieved (Supplementary-Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref>).

text.text: Physicians at participating hospitals validated individual datapoints by reviewing concept frequencies, terminology mappings, source attribution, and concordance between structured and unstructured sources.

Investigators then reviewed aggregated cohort outputs at site and consortium levels, iteratively assessing summary statistics, phenotype definitions, and variable distributions to identify inconsistencies, refine extraction rules, and update the FAIR-ICI data dictionary.
These validation procedures, together with predefined phenotype algorithms, aimed to minimize data extraction errors and misclassification.

The multidisciplinary FAIR-ICI team brought together clinical oncologists, epidemiologists, and clinical informatics specialists from participating hospitals and LynxCare to support data harmonization, validation, analysis, and clinical interpretation.
Baseline characteristics were summarized as medians with interquartile ranges (IQR) for continuous variables and frequencies and percentages for categorical variables.
Missing values were retained as a separate category.
OS, ToT, and TTNT were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method, reporting median times with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and survival probabilities at selected time points.
Differences between Kaplan-Meier curves were assessed using the log-rank test.
To explore factors associated with OS, a multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression model was fitted among patients with metastatic disease.
The model was stratified by cancer type to allow for cancer type-specific baseline hazards.
Adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CIs were reported.

To contextualize real-world outcomes, pivotal phase III randomized controlled trials were identified by cancer type and treatment regimen, focusing on combinations known to represent first-line treatment in routine clinical practice.
Published Kaplan-Meier survival estimates were digitized using WebPlotDigitizer and plotted alongside FAIR-ICI estimates for descriptive comparison.

The primary descriptive analyses and dashboard-based subgroup exploration were planned, while comparisons with pivotal clinical trials and post-discontinuation survival analyses were added during the study.

text.text: The cohort included patients receiving anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1, and anti-CTLA-4 therapies, either alone or in combination.
Overall, the cohort was predominantly older (59.7% aged ≥65 years) and male (62.5%) (Table 1).

text.text: ICI uptake increased over the years, from 185 patients during 2015-2017 to 598 in 2022.

Most patients had metastatic disease at treatment initiation (77.8%), but the number of patients receiving ICI in the non-metastatic setting increased markedly over time, from 5 patients (1.5% of ICI initiations) in 2018 to 71 (12.3%) in 2023.
Treatment patterns varied across cancer types.
ICI monotherapy was the most common regimen (55.0%), particularly in melanoma and urothelial carcinoma, whereas ICI combined with chemotherapy was more frequent in NSCLC.

Among metastatic patients (Figure 2A), the majority (62%, n=1,548) either died during treatment (23.9%, n=601) or initiated a new regimen within 12 weeks of the last ICI administration (37.7%, n=947), the latter potentially reflecting progression or toxicity.
text.formatted: Among metastatic patients (Figure <ref type="figure">2A</ref>), the majority (62%, n=1,548) either died during treatment (23.9%, n=601) or initiated a new regimen within 12 weeks of the last ICI administration (37.7%, n=947), the latter potentially reflecting progression or toxicity.

text.text: In contrast, 22.6% (n=568) discontinued ICI without subsequent treatment within 12 weeks, potentially reflecting deep remission or toxicity without the need or possibility for further treatment in the short term.
This was most frequent in melanoma (104/297, 35.0%) and RCC (39/190, 20.5%), consistent with known ICI efficacy, and least frequent in head and neck cancer (33/215, 15.3%).
Among patients permanently discontinuing ICI without subsequent treatment (Figure 2B), median postdiscontinuation OS was 21.4 months (95% CI 16.5-37.2).

text.text: Post-discontinuation survival was most favorable in melanoma (median not reached; 24-month OS 76.2%), followed by RCC (median 28.9 months, 95% CI 9.8-NR; 24-month OS 53.0%).
Corresponding 24-month OS estimates were 49.8% for NSCLC, 35.0% for urothelial carcinoma, and 26.6% for head and neck cancer.

Real-world survival and treatment outcomes Among metastatic patients, median OS varied substantially across the five major cancer types, ranging from 11 months in head and neck cancer and urothelial carcinoma to 78 months in melanoma (Table 2).

Among these five cancer types, OS event proportions ranged from 32.7% in melanoma to 66.0% in head and neck cancer, while median follow-up ranged from 7.6 months in head and neck cancer to 20.8 months in melanoma.

This discrepancy between treatment duration and survival was particularly pronounced in melanoma, where median OS reached 78 months despite a median ToT of 7 months and median TTNT of 26 months.
We compared real-world outcomes in unselected patient populations with pivotal clinical trials for all cancer type-regimen subgroups known to represent first-line treatment settings (Figure 3).

text.text: Real-world survival curves generally followed patterns similar to the corresponding pivotal clinical trials but were frequently less favorable, particularly during early follow-up.
The most pronounced visual discrepancies were observed in NSCLC treated with pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy, HCC with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab, and RCC with pembrolizumab plus TKI.
In contrast, closer alignment was observed for RCC and mesothelioma treated with ipilimumab plus nivolumab, and head and neck cancer treated with pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy.
Patients with ECOG 0-1 consistently showed longer OS than those with ECOG ≥2 (Figure 4), with significant differences in NSCLC, melanoma, RCC, and urothelial carcinoma, but not head and neck cancer.

text.text: Among patients with NSCLC receiving first-line pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy, survival in patients with ECOG 0-1 more closely approximated that reported in the pivotal KEYNOTE-189 trial, whereas patients with ECOG ≥2 had substantially poorer survival.
Additional Kaplan-Meier analyses by age, sex, BMI, smoking status, and alcohol abuse are presented in Supplementary-Figures S3-S7.

text.text: Modest differences in survival by age and sex were observed in selected cancers, particularly melanoma and RCC, although these patterns were not consistently significant across tumor types.
In contrast, associations with BMI, smoking status, and alcohol abuse were less consistent.
In multivariable Cox regression among metastatic patients (Table 3), older age, male sex, and ECOG ≥2 were associated with poorer OS.

text.text: ECOG ≥2 showed the strongest association with mortality (adjusted HR 2.18, 95% CI 1.82-2.60), while mortality increased progressively with age.
No clear associations were observed for BMI, smoking status, or alcohol abuse.

In this multicenter real-world cohort of 3,231 patients receiving ICIs across four Belgian hospitals, we described treatment utilization, trajectories, and clinical outcomes across multiple cancer types using an NLPenriched OMOP-CDM framework.
Several key findings warrant particular attention.

First, nearly one-quarter of metastatic patients permanently discontinued ICIs without initiating another systemic therapy within 12 weeks and nevertheless experienced prolonged survival (2-year OS 49% after stop).

Second, treatment-based endpoints (ToT and TTNT) were substantially shorter than OS across tumor types, suggesting that many patients remained alive long after treatment discontinuation and often before requiring additional therapy.
Third, real-world outcomes generally followed pivotal trial pattern but were frequently less favorable, emphasizing the need for complementary RWE alongside RCTs.
Finally, ECOG performance status emerged as one of the strongest prognostic factors across analyses, highlighting the importance of systematic assessment in routine oncology practice.
One of the most notable findings was that permanent ICI discontinuation did not necessarily indicate treatment failure or poor prognosis (Figure 2).
text.formatted: One of the most notable findings was that permanent ICI discontinuation did not necessarily indicate treatment failure or poor prognosis (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: Although discontinuation reasons require further validation, preliminary analyses suggest a heterogeneous mixture of treatment-related toxicity, disease progression, patient preference, and sustained disease control without immediate need for subsequent systemic therapy.
Favorable post-discontinuation outcomes, particularly in melanoma and RCC, suggest durable benefit beyond active treatment in a subset of patients.
These observations are consistent with growing evidence that durable disease control can persist after treatment cessation.
ICIs may promote durable antitumor immune memory, sustaining T-cell-mediated tumor control beyond active treatment.
Optimal duration of ICI treatment remains uncertain, with pivotal trials generally continuing treatment until progression, unacceptable toxicity, or a maximum of two years.
In melanoma, long-term trial evidence has demonstrated durable disease control and survival following ICI therapy 18, 19 .

text.text: RWE further showed low relapse after elective anti-PD-1 discontinuation among patients achieving complete response after more than six months of treatment 20 , while a recent emulated target trial suggested that around one year may be sufficient in patients with disease control 21 .

text.text: Similarly, in metastatic RCC, elective discontinuation after approximately two years did not appear to compromise long-term outcomes among responding patients 22 .

text.text: Collectively, these findings suggest that cessation does not necessarily indicate loss of clinical benefit and highlight the need for further investigation of optimal ICI duration in routine practice 23.

text.text: The discrepancy observed between OS and treatment-trajectory endpoints further supports this interpretation.

Across tumor types, median ToT and TTNT were consistently shorter than OS (Table 2), indicating that many patients remained alive for prolonged periods after treatment discontinuation and often before requiring subsequent systemic therapy.

text.text: These findings suggest that treatment duration, switching, and survival capture distinct aspects of real-world treatment trajectories.

Consequently, ToT and TTNT should be considered complementary treatment-trajectory endpoints that provide information distinct from OS, such as health care consumption, when evaluating real-world immunotherapy outcomes 12, 24.

text.text: Compared with pivotal clinical trials, real-world survival was frequently less favorable, particularly during early follow-up.
The most pronounced visual discrepancies were observed in NSCLC treated with pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy, HCC with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab, and RCC with pembrolizumab plus TKI (Figure 3).
text.formatted: The most pronounced visual discrepancies were observed in NSCLC treated with pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy, HCC with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab, and RCC with pembrolizumab plus TKI (Figure <ref type="figure">3</ref>).

text.text: These findings are consistent with the well-recognized differences between trial populations and routine clinical practice.

Pivotal trials often employ restrictive eligibility criteria that exclude patients with poor performance status, substantial comorbidities, organ dysfunction, autoimmune disease, or advanced age, thereby limiting the representativeness of enrolled populations 9, 10, 25 .
text.formatted: Pivotal trials often employ restrictive eligibility criteria that exclude patients with poor performance status, substantial comorbidities, organ dysfunction, autoimmune disease, or advanced age, thereby limiting the representativeness of enrolled populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">25</ref> .

text.text: Recent analyses also identified prognostic heterogeneity as an important explanation, with high-risk real-world patients experiencing substantially poorer survival than would be predicted from pivotal trials 26 .
text.formatted: Recent analyses also identified prognostic heterogeneity as an important explanation, with high-risk real-world patients experiencing substantially poorer survival than would be predicted from pivotal trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">26</ref> .

text.text: Our ECOG-stratified analysis of NSCLC patients receiving pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy further illustrates this (Figure 4).
text.formatted: Our ECOG-stratified analysis of NSCLC patients receiving pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy further illustrates this (Figure <ref type="figure">4</ref>).

text.text: Survival with ECOG 0-1 more closely approximated KEYNOTE-189, whereas patients with ECOG ≥2 had substantially poorer survival, suggesting that performance status contributes to trial-real-world differences.
The observed RCC treatment patterns further highlight the complexity of interpreting real-world comparative effectiveness.
While outcomes with nivolumab plus ipilimumab were broadly comparable to CheckMate214, early survival with pembrolizumab plus TKI appeared less favorable than in KEYNOTE-426.
Although the number of patients receiving pembrolizumab plus TKI was small (n=24) and no comparative conclusions can be drawn, one possible explanation is confounding by indication.

In routine practice, ICI-TKI combinations may be preferentially selected for patients with higher disease burden, more symptomatic disease, or a need for rapid disease control, given the high response rate (59.3%) and early tumor responses in metastatic RCC 27 .

text.text: Consequently, patients receiving apparently similar first-line therapies in real-world settings may differ substantially in underlying prognosis, introducing biases that are difficult to fully capture using routinely collected data 26 .

text.text: This underscores the importance of considering treatment-selection processes and baseline prognosis when interpreting real-world comparative effectiveness studies.

Prognostic factors and the importance of ECOG performance status Among the prognostic factors evaluated, ECOG performance status emerged as the strongest predictor of survival in both subgroup and multivariable analyses (Figure 4; Table 3).
text.formatted: Prognostic factors and the importance of ECOG performance status Among the prognostic factors evaluated, ECOG performance status emerged as the strongest predictor of survival in both subgroup and multivariable analyses (Figure <ref type="figure">4</ref>; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>).

text.text: Patients with ECOG ≥2 had more than twice the hazard of death compared with ECOG 0-1, consistent with extensive literature identifying functional status as a major determinant of outcomes in patients receiving immunotherapy [28] [29] [30] [31] .

text.text: This is particularly relevant because pivotal trials predominantly enrolled patients with ECOG 0-1, whereas routine clinical practice includes a broader spectrum of patients, including those with impaired functional status.
Consequently, performance status may contribute substantially to the differences observed between trial and real-world outcomes 9.
text.formatted: Consequently, performance status may contribute substantially to the differences observed between trial and real-world outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">9</ref>.

text.text: Notably, ECOG performance status was unavailable for a substantial proportion of patients in our cohort (59%), reflecting a common limitation of routinely collected data.

Nevertheless, the strong and consistent association observed among patients with available data suggests that performance status may explain an important component of outcome heterogeneity in routine practice.
Given its strong prognostic value, more systematic capture of ECOG in EHRs should be prioritized to improve risk adjustment and interpretability of future real-world studies.

The ability of FAIR-ICI to extract ECOG information through NLP-enhanced extraction from unstructured clinical documentation highlights the value of integrating structured and unstructured data sources for oncology RWE.

Beyond performance status, older age and male sex were associated with poorer OS in the multivariable analysis (Table 3), although differences were generally modest in cancer-specific Kaplan-Meier analyses (Supplementary-Figures S3-S4).
text.formatted: Beyond performance status, older age and male sex were associated with poorer OS in the multivariable analysis (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>), although differences were generally modest in cancer-specific Kaplan-Meier analyses (Supplementary-Figures <ref type="figure">S3-S4</ref>).

text.text: Associations with BMI, smoking status, and alcohol abuse were less evident, with no clear associations observed after adjustment.
To our knowledge, FAIR-ICI represents the first multicenter immunotherapy-focused RWE platform integrating structured and unstructured EHR data within a standardized OMOP-CDM framework.

By combining data from four hospitals and incorporating NLP-derived clinical variables, FAIR-ICI enabled evaluation of treatment trajectories and outcomes across multiple tumor types with greater clinical granularity than typically available in administrative or registry-based datasets.
The reuse of routinely collected clinical data also enables largescale analyses without additional burden to patients or resource-intensive prospective data collection.
Furthermore, the publicly available interactive dashboard supports transparent exploration of results and facilitates subgroup analyses by clinicians, researchers, and policymakers.
Several limitations should be acknowledged.
First, the retrospective observational design is inherently susceptible to residual confounding and treatment-selection bias.

In particular, treatment allocation in routine clinical practice may be influenced by factors that were not fully captured in the available data, including disease burden, symptom severity, physician preference, and other clinical considerations, potentially resulting in confounding by indication.
Second, several variables contained substantial missingness, particularly ECOG performance status and some lifestyle characteristics.
Missing ECOG data may also introduce bias if their availability is associated with patient prognosis.
Third, treatment line could not always be determined directly, and selected trial comparisons therefore relied on treatment-regimen subgroups considered likely to represent first-line settings.
Fourth, reasons for treatment discontinuation were not directly assessed, limiting interpretation of the clinical circumstances underlying ICI cessation.
Further characterization of discontinuation reasons and treatment-related toxicity represents an important direction for future FAIR-ICI analyses.
Finally, despite including four hospitals, several cancer type-treatment subgroups remained small, limiting the precision of subgroup analyses and restricting interpretation.
Belgium's broad ICI access and the inclusion of academic and regional hospitals support the relevance of these findings to routine oncology practice.
However, differences in reimbursement policies, patient characteristics, and data availability may limit generalizability to other healthcare systems.
This multicenter real-world study provides a comprehensive overview of immunotherapy utilization, treatment trajectories, and outcomes across multiple cancer types.

A notable proportion of patients remained alive for prolonged periods after treatment discontinuation without subsequent systemic therapy, highlighting the potential for durable clinical benefit beyond active treatment exposure.
Differences between OS, ToT, and TTNT demonstrate that these endpoints capture distinct, complementary dimensions of immunotherapy benefit.

While real-world outcomes broadly mirrored those observed in pivotal clinical trials, they were frequently less favorable, underscoring the importance of understanding differences between trial populations and routine practice.

ECOG performance status was strongly associated with survival, emphasizing the importance of functional status in immunotherapy-treated populations and the need for its systematic capture in real-world datasets.
The interactive dashboard further enables exploration of FAIR-ICI findings across clinically relevant patient subgroups.

Together, these findings establish FAIR-ICI as a valuable RWE platform for future investigations, particularly for extending the dataset into treatment toxicity and reasons for treatment discontinuation, as well as treatment sequencing, and biomarker-driven precision immuno-oncology.
